items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] How fast-food workers are being ranked and reprimanded with AI
items.content_html:
Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see.

The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting-edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering, and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney said.

As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.” 

Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer, and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos, franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime’s ability to track workers in real time, down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website, by having workers compete for better scores. 

Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment. 

Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior—how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom—into data that can score, rank, discipline, and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers, and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring. 

“They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools.

* * *

In February, Burger King announced that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders. 

“It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez.

Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly. 

Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added. 

Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini” [Google’s AI assistant].

“The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.”

Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations time-stamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores. 

Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.” 

According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities. 

Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity, or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias. 

The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year.

Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it. 

He quit in August.

 “If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.”

* * *

While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies—Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC, and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts”—a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility.

Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys, and other chains. 

Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock, or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts.

In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law.

Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.”

* * *

While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores, and ranks all employees.

Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests,” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange, they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions.

When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores. 

Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored, and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.”

MashMore currently has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.”

* * *

Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on September 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff.

Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty—but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.” 

Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.”

Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off. 

When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing.

Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.”

—By Z Waite

This piece was originally published by Capital & Main.

items.title: [arxiv.org] Study finds coding-agent instruction files grow 226% over time
items.content_html:
A new study of AI coding-agent instructions found that files such as CLAUDE.md grew by 226% over their lifetimes as additions outpaced deletions across 1,867 repositories. Researcher Kushal Chakrabarti analyzed 247,694 instruction lifetimes and attributed the pattern to agents’ imperfect recall of why older instructions were added.

The paper, revised Nov. 20, reports that comments recording the reasoning behind instructions cut excess prompt size by 99.3% in constructed tests. In small-scale tests in real repositories, the approach also improved instruction-following by 17.7%. The coding agent Claude Code is also being used for projects beyond conventional software development, including hobbyist-built apps and hardware prototypes. A separate review of the free coding agent Freebuff warns that it logs mouse and keyboard input and may use submitted information for advertising and AI training.

Google reported that attackers exploited two PaperCut print-server flaws in August, with one campaign reaching hundreds of organizations four days after disclosure. Amazon separately documented an AI-assisted intrusion using Cairn that targeted East Asian educational institutions in September. The U.S. Government Accountability Office said AI reduces the human effort needed for complex attacks and cited a fully autonomous ransomware operation. Google says these systems currently sacrifice stealth for speed but expects attacks to become harder to detect. items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] CrowdStrike CEO: Companies are choosing between getting hacked and shutting down
items.content_html:
Microsoft systems down. Air traffic systems down. Problems at Chase, United, and Apple. After a week of outages across big systems, the AI conspiracy theories are in full swing. CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz describes how AI agents can turn a patch into a working exploit within an hour, and how CEOs are now taking services offline rather than risk being hacked. He also discusses CrowdStrike’s new AI Kill Switch, and why slowing down the frontier labs won’t slow down the attackers.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

So what is going on? Over the past week, we’ve seen Microsoft systems go down. Air traffic systems go down. . . . The AI conspiracy theories are everywhere. Is all this just a coincidence?

I think a few of my friends and colleagues might have their tinfoil hats on as well. The reality is it’s the bill for the Mythos moment. Nine months ago, when Mythos came out, it really set in motion everyone looking for these vulnerabilities, right? And the whole industry has been racing to find as many vulnerabilities as it can and create as many patches as it can. But what we’ve done now is hit the sound barrier of actually being able to roll out all these patches. So when you look at what’s really taking place, and you look at all the issues that were found in Black October, you’ve got Darker November.

This is like the PHP code, and now Java, that people are scrambling to find and plug these gaps in.

Yeah, exactly. I think the Java one is actually going to be worse. There are already working exploits for all of that. But what people are doing now is rushing to roll out all of these patches, and they’re making the decision: Breach or break. That is, are we going to get breached because we can’t patch fast enough, or are we just going to break something and hopefully fix it if we roll it out? That’s kind of a new norm now because the industry can’t keep up.

Technology is messy. Things happen, and we’re going to get better and better as an industry at dealing with this sort of AI speed that we’re facing. When you think about all the legacy systems that are out there, and you think about even banking-type systems, there’s a lot of legacy-type code out there, and it’s not as easy just to create a fix while everything is in midstream. So it’s not always clear, and when things are melting down, you get on these 24-hour bridges, and people are trying to figure out what actually happened. It’s a bit of fog of war.

As you describe it and go through these examples, the air traffic one seems like a particularly fragile one. Is the system fragile?

I think technology is just fragile, whether you’re in an Apple ecosystem, Android, or you use Microsoft or Google, whatever you’re using. Every day people use this, and they sort of just expect it to work, and they should. But behind the scenes, when you actually look at how complicated these systems are, how they operate, and the interaction with hardware and software, disks get full, memory gets overloaded. You would think that all this has been worked out, but there’s a lot of just making stuff work in the background. And the technology folks, the men and women who have to keep this running, literally wake up every day and are just like, “OK, what are we going to have to deal with today?”

We’ve had other kinds of cyber troubles recently: OpenAI’s agents breaking into Hugging Face, and French supermarkets hit by hackers shutting down refrigeration systems, which seem like a different order of things. Are any of these episodes an “aha” moment for you, of us sort of crossing a threshold?

When you look at the latest Patch Tuesday from Microsoft, it was 1,000-plus vulnerabilities that were fixed. And again, this has spiked. . . . I think we’ve had 25% of all the vulnerabilities ever created found in the last year. Just to give you an idea of the order of magnitude of what we have to deal with.

So all these patches come out, and now what we’re seeing is the automation by AI agents and threat actors, where they will take a patch and compare what was patched versus what wasn’t patched, and they immediately know where the flaw was. Then they automate the vulnerability exploitation of that. Within an hour, you can have all that done, where that would take a nation-state actor maybe weeks to do.

So the fact that we’re starting to see these issues come up as quickly as we are, I’m not surprised. But when you think about the refrigeration systems, this was a big one in Europe. What does AI allow you to do? There’s probably a handful of people, relatively speaking, on planet Earth who understand how to program these refrigeration systems. But when you actually take an AI agent and go, “Hey, I don’t know much about the refrigeration system. You figure out how to program it,” it will figure that out. You don’t have to be an expert in any of these technologies now. And typically they’re underprotected because it’s a refrigerator. Nobody really thought about security when they were building it.

How much of the game is becoming like “My AI is better than their AI?” You have to stay ahead of the attacks.

It’s the old Spy vs. Spy cartoon. It’s really what it is, right? Who’s going to stay ahead?

You recently launched a product called the AI Kill Switch. Which is designed to stop rogue agents. How do you know which scenarios would prompt hitting the kill switch?

If you think about industry, if there was a manufacturing problem with a big machine, there’s always the red button. It’s like, stop that thing because it could be causing bodily harm. And it’s the same scenario. Are the agents doing something they shouldn’t be doing? Are they multiplying, attacking other systems, or bringing down systems internally? You want to be able to hit the button. The challenge with the kill switch is there’s blunt force. It’s almost like pulling the plug.

You work closely with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Dario Amodei at Anthropic has called on the industry to slow down. There’s been quite a lot of noise about it, although development keeps steaming ahead. Do you give OpenAI and Anthropic advice about speeding versus slowing?

At the end of the day, the genie is out of the bottle. You can slow whatever you want down on the frontier. The open-weight models are three months behind. Just slowing them down is not going to slow the rest of the world down. But keep in mind, and I just want to make this distinction, Bob, they are called labs. Okay, labs. What happens in a lab? You develop something, it kind of works, it does great things, but when you put it in the real world, it may not actually work as intended in the lab, which is why the security industry has now moved into the safety industry and has become a great opportunity for folks like us.

Anyone can slow down. If the model is not right, if it’s not aligned, if it’s not getting the output you want, if the quality control is not there, you know what you do? You don’t release it. You go back and do another run until you get it right.

So what should any business leader do right now to improve their cyber footing?

Well, I think maybe first is go find your security and IT people and give them a hug, because they are at 110% of capacity now. I’ve never seen this before, but it’s happening across industry. Company CEOs are making a decision: Take something offline or be hacked. They’re saying, “Hey, we would rather take a massive service offline than be hacked.” They’re willing to make that decision if it’s so bad. When PHP came out, I had plenty of companies say, “Hey, we may just take everything down because it’s so bad.”

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools
items.content_html:
Over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the company announced two new switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics.

The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help users avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just shows less.

Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like.

Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off.

The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company says its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics.

Why, really

The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library.

These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement.

In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.”

But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The company says that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.”

Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company.

Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as quickly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”

items.content_html:
Macworld

The U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government must confirm that it demanded access to Apple customers’ data in 2025.

Early last year, the Washington Post was tipped off about the secret order, or “technical capability notice,” which ordered Apple to “create a back door allowing [U.K. authorities] to retrieve all the content any Apple user worldwide has uploaded to the cloud.” At the time, we warned that such an order would instantly compromise the security of more than two billion Apple users across the globe.

Apple resisted, choosing to remove the ADP feature from U.K. iPhones rather than comply with the order, and it was subsequently reported that British politicians had given up on the scheme. But while it was common knowledge that the attempt had been made, the Home Office refused to acknowledge this, arguing that revealing the existence of the order would damage national security and the public interest.

Apple itself was not permitted to disclose that it had received a technical capability notice. Until now the company has adhered to this even while commenting in carefully non-specific terms on the situation. At one point, for example, it stated that “we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products, and we never will” without actually confirming it had been ordered to do so in this case.

But now, finally, as TechCrunch reports, the national security argument has been put to rest.

Having noted that “anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges indicate that they “reject the respondent’s contention that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the fact that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice.”

It should be noted that this judgment refers to the existence of the order rather than its specific details. The judges say this is “another matter” which “is better addressed separately.” The case, in other words, is not finished yet.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals a strategy to undercut its AI rivals
items.content_html:
Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

‘Compute multipliers’ and ‘Anthropic Direct’ may be the IPO’s secret sauce

As frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google converge in capabilities, the companies selling them may end up competing for enterprise business less on model quality and more on the cost of the computing power needed to run them. In its IPO filing and investor roadshow video, Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, suggested it may be preparing for that future with something called “compute multipliers” and a compute-sourcing model it calls Anthropic Direct.

In its S-1, filed publicly in October, Anthropic defines compute multipliers as “algorithmic and methodological” improvements in the way it trains and operates models, effectively increasing the computing power it can get from a given amount of capacity. And these multipliers are “stackable.” In its roadshow video, Anthropic says it measures “total effective compute,” which is its physical computing capacity multiplied by the multipliers it has discovered or expects to discover in the future. Its example: If a model takes 100 units of compute to train, a 4x multiplier lets Anthropic train the same model with 25 units, or use all 100 units to train a model that would previously have required 400.

The company also says the multipliers “stack,” with each new discovery building on previous ones, and that it expects Claude will eventually be able to discover multipliers on its own.

According to the filing, the gains apply to models used to serve customers as well as to model training. Anthropic says its researchers “have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference,” reducing the computing power needed to deliver a given level of model performance. The company says this “allows us to provide greater value for customers.”

Anthropic has already been cutting prices. It says price reductions tied to new model versions, along with contractual discounts, reduced revenue growth by about $600 million between the second and third quarters of 2026. It says Opus 5.5, launched in September, delivered “a lower cost per task” than earlier models. If Anthropic can get more usable compute out of each chip than its rivals can, it may be able to undercut other AI labs on price. It may also be able to undercut cloud providers that sell AI services built on their own models.

If compute multipliers let Anthropic do more with its physical computing power, Anthropic Direct could give the company greater control over where that power comes from. Right now, Anthropic buys almost all its computing power from cloud providers, including competitors like SpaceX, Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, and CoreWeave. The company says it has already committed to buying roughly $900.9 billion in compute from these providers over the coming years and decades. Those expenses also include short-term cloud compute purchases, mainly to cover peak usage periods, which come at a premium.

The S-1 says Anthropic is reducing its reliance on expensive cloud providers by developing its own data centers and leasing the chips that go inside them. Its first Anthropic Direct facility came online this year. The company says a “significant portion” of its planned compute spending will go toward building more Anthropic Direct capacity. Based on an analysis of contract values in the S-1 filing, PitchBook estimates that Direct data centers will supply about 1% of Anthropic’s available compute capacity this year, 48% in 2030, and 60% in 2035.

The S-1 says Anthropic’s total compute pool, including third-party cloud compute and Direct, will be used for its own research and model development, as well as customer workloads. Bringing more compute in-house could dramatically reduce the overhead costs of developing and serving Claude models, apps, and agents for enterprise and consumer customers. That, in turn, could allow Anthropic to lower per-token prices for enterprises and subscription rates for consumers.

But Anthropic Direct may end up being something more. The filing doesn’t specifically say Direct compute could be rented to enterprise customers. Still, it’s a possibility; Anthropic could be building an AI-native cloud where enterprises could store their proprietary data and run Anthropic’s models in the same secure environment, potentially at a lower cost than building the same setup within an Amazon, Google, or Microsoft cloud.

That would give the Anthropic Direct brand name a very different meaning. Instead of accessing Claude models through a cloud provider they already use, customers would come directly to Anthropic. That could turn computing from a major overhead expense into a service Anthropic controls and rents to others for profit—a significant change to the company’s business model.

Some big obstacles stand in the way of such an ambition. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are currently Anthropic’s largest compute suppliers, as well as the main distribution channels through which enterprises buy Claude. The S-1 notes that the three companies are at once Anthropic’s “investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors.” If Anthropic challenged their cloud businesses directly, it would almost certainly strain those relationships. On the other hand, as more Direct data centers come online, Anthropic’s dependence on those cloud partners could decrease.

If the current rough parity among frontier models continues, the company that can deliver intelligence at the lowest overall cost per task—not per token—may have the edge. Anthropic’s filing suggests it is working toward that position on two fronts: getting more out of each chip and controlling more of the infrastructure those chips run on. Have retail investors factored that strategy into the price they’re willing to pay for Anthropic stock? The answer may emerge only after the stock has traded for a week or so.

California sues OpenAI over rogue AI agents

The California attorney general, Rob Bonta, sued OpenAI on Monday, alleging the company developed and tested advanced AI models without adequate safeguards. The suit centers on a July incident in which OpenAI agents escaped a testing environment and breached the systems of AI platform Hugging Face.

The complaint says OpenAI told the state it has lost control of its autonomous agents more than 80 times during testing. Bonta called the Hugging Face attack the “predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI” that puts growth ahead of safety. The state alleges violations of California’s unfair competition law and seeks an injunction, civil penalties, and disgorgement of profits. An OpenAI spokesperson said the suit “appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab.”

Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia CEO. Its board says nah

Nvidia’s board rejected the idea of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO just hours after Huang said on Twitter that he’d be “honored” to return. On the company’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon, Harvey Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation. He has drawn support from Elon Musk, President Trump, and a petition with about 180,000 signatures, but the board is continuing its search for a permanent successor. Colette Kress, the CFO, is serving as interim CEO.

Huang broke his silence Tuesday, less than a week after resigning amid a personal conduct scandal and an investigation. In a statement on X, he said that if the board decides his return is in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company, and America, “I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang acknowledged making “serious mistakes in my personal life,” and said, “I own my mistakes completely.” He also said he is “committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” 

Demis Hassabis’s Isomorphic Labs raises $5 billion

Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug-discovery company founded and led by Demis Hassabis and spun out of Google DeepMind, announced a $5 billion Series C round of funding on Tuesday. Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital led the round, with participation from Andreessen Horowitz and other new investors and continued significant investment from Alphabet. Several existing backers—Thrive Capital, MGX, GV, CapitalG, Temasek, and the U.K. Sovereign AI Fund—also invested.

Isomorphic will use the money to scale IsoDDE, its drug-design engine built on AlphaFold-related technology, and to push drug candidates toward clinical trials. In a post on X, Hassabis said the company continues “to make rapid progress reimagining drug design from first principles with AI” to cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. No valuation was disclosed, but Bloomberg had reported the company was in talks to base the round on a valuation of about $50 billion.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] As widespread tech outages pile up, AI tools are in the spotlight again
items.content_html:
Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions.

In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal.

Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government’s Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was “zero” indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals.

The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches.

Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages.

“To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it’s made them realize how many parts of their lives they’ve handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don’t fully understand,” Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. “I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way.”

What’s gone offline recently

Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors.

Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a “latent defect” in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer.

For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA’s network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday.

Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved.

And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app.

Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday “during scheduled routine maintenance.”

The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there’s no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack.

Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from “AI / agents,” although it didn’t immediately specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. Microsoft did not respond to an Associated Press request for further details, and the other companies did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email.

AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks

AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps.

For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays.

President Donald Trump’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA’s outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month’s PHP alert has caused some systems to “not come back up” as expected. “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said.

Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it.

At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions.

“As AI adoption accelerates, we are likely to witness more incidents of this nature,” Raj Rajarajan, director of the Institute for Cyber Security at City St George’s, University of London, said last week.

He noted a lot of today’s digital infrastructure wasn’t originally designed to handle the “computational demands of large-scale AI services.”

While recent outages haven’t been tied to hackers or a coordinated attack, he and others also pointed to cybersecurity risks more broadly.

“AI is absolutely making it way easier for attackers to go and launch cyber attacks. It is not quite as good at creating patches for bugs, like fixing problems, as it is exploiting them,” said Justin Cappos, a cybersecurity professor at New York University’s Tandon School of Engineering.

In a cybersecurity report this week, Google said hackers and cyber criminals are “moving beyond basic prompting” and using increasingly sophisticated AI techniques to devise and carry out their attacks. The report, which focused on nefarious activity rather than outages, said techniques include using large language models and “agentic frameworks” to reverse engineering security patches to uncover vulnerabilities and exploit them.

Unraveling one (of just a few) major players in our online lives

Regardless, the latest outages offer yet more examples of the cascading effects that can erupt when a central player in tech, banking, travel or even the government runs into system errors that upend services.

Democratic Sen. Mark Warner, co-chair of the U.S. Senate’s Cybersecurity Caucus, acknowledged the widespread concern — and again stressed what this means in the AI era.

“These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said Tuesday. He also argued that the Trump administration hadn’t shown enough interest in confronting these challenges.

Still, “based on what we know today, there is good reason to believe these disruptions are the unintended consequences of efforts to make our systems safer,” Warner added.

—Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, AP Business Writers

items.title: [ft.com] UK tribunal orders disclosure of secret Apple data-access notice
items.content_html: The UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled on Nov. 19 that the government could not keep secret a notice requiring Apple to give authorities access to encrypted customer data. The Home Office acknowledged issuing it. The judges rejected the claim that confirming the notice would harm national security, saying the government had not established that risk. The ruling addresses disclosure, not whether the government has the legal power to make the demand or what technical changes it requires. Those details remain secret, and a substantive hearing is expected in 2027. The dispute began with a January 2025 demand for access to users’ data worldwide, which Britain later withdrew after negotiations with the Trump administration. A second notice, issued in July 2026 and reportedly limited to UK customers, prompted Apple’s renewed challenge. Apple had already stopped offering its Advanced Data Protection encryption feature to new UK users in February 2025.

items.title: [MacRumors] UK Loses Secrecy Fight Over Apple 'Backdoor' Order
items.content_html:
Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

The government's position relied on its policy of neither confirming nor denying such notices. However, the tribunal found that disclosures to the media, including the Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

The ruling means that much of the legal action brought by Apple, alongside a separate challenge from Privacy International and Liberty, can proceed in open court.

Apple filed its latest legal challenge in July, following a second TCN. The Home Office had previously agreed to withdraw an earlier demand covering UK and U.S. customers after a dispute with the American government. The replacement notice is believed to focus on UK users specifically.

The dispute led Apple to stop offering Advanced Data Protection to new users in the UK in February 2025. The iCloud feature provides end-to-end encryption for additional categories of data, including device backups, photos, and notes, meaning Apple does not hold the keys needed to decrypt them.

UK users who had not already enabled ADP can no longer turn it on. Apple says it cannot switch the feature off on their behalf, so it can remain active on accounts where users previously enabled it and have not turned it off. The company said affected users will be given a period to disable ADP themselves to continue using ‌iCloud‌, but a deadline has still not been provided.

Without ADP, those additional categories of ‌iCloud‌ data use standard protection, under which Apple holds the encryption keys and can provide data in response to valid legal demands. iMessage and FaceTime remain end-to-end encrypted, as do categories protected by default, such as passwords and Health data.

The tribunal will now be able to hear much of the arguments over the government's encryption demands in public, with the legality of those demands still to be decided. Privacy International lists the substantive hearing for its separate challenge as scheduled for December 2026.

items.title: [hu.euronews.com] IEA warns AI data-centre boom could strain grids and raise costs
items.content_html: Electricity networks could struggle to connect a rapidly growing number of data centres, the International Energy Agency (IEA), a global energy watchdog, said in its World Energy Outlook published Nov. 19. Grid upgrades could delay projects and raise questions about who pays for new infrastructure. The IEA expects data-centre electricity use to double by 2030, with artificial intelligence driving three-quarters of the increase. It also warned that planned developments in some markets could exceed current peak power demand. In France, about 80 data-centre projects had reserved nearly 18 gigawatts of grid capacity by May 2026, while connected sites were using, on average, about one-fifth of the power they had requested. A regional study put the average cost of connecting to the transmission grid at about €30 million, with some costs covered by regulated network charges. French grid operator RTE is planning shared development zones to spread infrastructure costs among users. The IEA identified underuse, early exit and cancellation as financial risks. Regulators are seeking guarantees and minimum payments to limit losses if projects are abandoned.

Agricultural companies, researchers and farmers are using artificial intelligence for crop monitoring, breeding, irrigation and farm administration, as tools move from research into field trials. A survey previewed at the PLUSAGRI 2026 conference in Warsaw on Nov. 18 found that 53.9% of participating Polish farmers said they use AI; organizers planned to present findings on how farmers use the technology and how much they trust it. Sweden’s Lantmännen says it uses AI in plant breeding and to improve the use of fertilizer, crop protection products and water. Applications range from software that analyzes crop images and farm data to AI-guided irrigation. A European potato program supported by Cropin examined how farming practices affect water use and potato quality, while researchers have reported AI systems that identify crop models from agricultural data. A Chinese provincial study analyzed data from 2005 to 2023, while newer tools still require testing across crops and climates before broader use.
